title: Does a skydiver keep speeding up?
hook: Gravity never lets go of a falling skydiver. So why does her speed stop growing?

knows: air pushes back on moving things
doesNotKnow: that drag grows with the square of speed
that speed levels off when drag equals weight (terminal velocity)

misconception: A falling body keeps accelerating until it hits the ground.
objective: The learner can explain that drag grows with speed until it equals weight, after which the net force is zero and speed stops growing.

claims.text: Air drag on a skydiver grows with the square of speed, F = 1/2 rho C_d A v^2.
claims.source: Quadratic drag law at high Reynolds number; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 6 (drag force and terminal speed).

claims.text: Speed stops growing when drag equals weight: v_t = sqrt(2 m g / (rho C_d A)).
claims.source: Set 1/2 rho C_d A v^2 = m g (zero net force, Newton's second law).

claims.text: For 80 kg belly-down (C_d A = 0.7 m^2) the limit is 43.2 m/s, about 156 km/h; head-down (C_d A = 0.3 m^2) it is 66.0 m/s.
claims.source: sqrt(2 x 80 x 9.81 / (1.2 x 0.7)) = 43.23 m/s (x 3.6 = 155.6 km/h); sqrt(2 x 80 x 9.81 / (1.2 x 0.3)) = 66.03 m/s. The predict option says 'near 43 m/s (155 km/h)'.

claims.text: Belly-down at 80 kg she reaches 42.3 m/s after 10 s, within 3% of the limit; head-down takes about 15 s to come within 3%.
claims.source: RK4 integration of m dv/dt = m g - 1/2 rho C_d A v^2 from rest, dt = 0.01 s (in Demo.tsx): belly 35.1 m/s at 5 s, 42.3 at 10 s (97.9%); head-down 59.6 at 10 s (90.3%), 64.5 at 15 s (97.7%). Analytic check: v = v_t tanh(g t / v_t) gives 42.3 m/s at 10 s.

claims.text: Model: air density held at 1.2 kg/m^3 (sea level) and C_d A values of 0.7 and 0.3 m^2 are typical estimates, not measurements of one person.
claims.source: Stated idealisation (brief cm-physics #13). Real jumps from about 4 km start in thinner air (about 0.8 kg/m^3), so real early speeds run higher; commonly quoted belly-to-earth terminal speeds are about 50-55 m/s (e.g. USPA skydiving references), which this toy model's 0.7 m^2 underestimates.

claims.text: A heavier skydiver has a higher limit speed, growing as the square root of mass.
claims.source: v_t proportional to sqrt(m) at fixed C_d A and rho: 50 kg gives 34.2 m/s, 120 kg gives 52.9 m/s belly-down.

recall.question: A raindrop falls from a high cloud. Halfway down, what is happening to its speed?
options: Still growing by 9.8 m/s every second
Steady: air drag has grown to match its weight
Shrinking: drag is now larger than its weight
recall.why: Drag grows with speed until it equals the weight; then the net force is zero and the speed stays steady.
